md: An appliance joins the mains by two wires: the **live** wire brings the supply in and the **neutral** wire completes the circuit. Touch the live wire and a current can pass through you. The **earth** wire carries no current in normal use: it is a safety route, joined to a metal case.

stem: The figure shows an appliance on the mains. Give the job of each of its three wires. [3]

steps.working: Live: brings the supply in at 230 V, through the fuse and the switch.
steps.decision: It is joined to the supply, so touching it lets a current pass through you.

steps.working: Neutral: carries the current back, completing the circuit.
steps.decision: The return path, close to 0 V.

steps.working: Earth: carries no current in normal use, and joins the metal case to earth.
steps.decision: A safety route, used only in a fault.

prompt: A fault joins one of an appliance's wires to its metal case. Which wire, touching the case, makes the case dangerous to hold?
explain: Step 1 of the See it: the live wire brings the supply in at 230 V, so a case joined to it is at 230 V and a current could pass through you. The neutral only carries the current back, and the earth carries none. So it is the live wire.

optionNotes.why: The neutral carries current too, so it can seem dangerous, but it is the return path, near 0 V: the push comes from the live wire.
The earth wire is joined to the case on purpose, as the safety route; it carries nothing in normal use.

twin.prompt: Which wire in a working appliance's cable normally carries no current?
twin.explain: The earth wire carries current only in a fault. The live brings the current in and the neutral carries it back, all the time the appliance runs.

optionNotes.why: The live wire carries the current in whenever the appliance is on.
The neutral carries the current back, so it carries it whenever the appliance is on.

caption: The same oscilloscope, two supplies: d.c. stays on one side of zero; a.c. crosses zero again and again.

md: A cell gives **direct current (d.c.)**: it flows in **one direction only**, a flat line on one side of zero on an oscilloscope (**CRO**). The mains gives **alternating current (a.c.)**: it **changes direction**, over and over, **regularly**, so its CRO trace rises above zero and falls below it.
One rise and fall is one cycle, and the UK mains makes 50 cycles a second: 50 hertz. The current changes direction twice a cycle: 50 × 2 = 100 times every second.

stem: Two traces are on a CRO. Trace X is a flat line two squares above the zero line. Trace Y is a wave that goes two squares above the zero line and two below it. Which trace is a.c., which is d.c., and why? [3]

steps.working: Trace X never crosses zero: its current flows one way only. It is d.c.
steps.decision: A flat line on one side of zero is one direction, steady.

steps.working: Trace Y crosses zero again and again: its current changes direction, regularly. It is a.c.
steps.decision: Each crossing of the zero line is a change of direction.

steps.working: X could come from a cell, and Y from the mains.
steps.decision: A cell or battery gives d.c.; the mains gives a.c.

title: GCSE Physics - Alternating Current & Direct Current
why: The two kinds of current and their traces, moving. It is made for another board: its potential difference is CCEA's voltage, and peak voltage and the National Grid are not on the CCEA specification.

prompt: On a CRO screen with a zero line across the middle, which trace shows alternating current?
options: a wave that crosses the zero line
a flat line above the zero line
a wave that stays above the zero line
answer: a wave that crosses the zero line
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, a.c. changes direction, and on a CRO a change of direction is a crossing of the zero line. A flat line is d.c., and a wave that never crosses zero never changes direction. So the a.c. trace is the wave that crosses the zero line.

optionNotes.option: a flat line above the zero line
optionNotes.why: That is a cell's d.c.: one direction, steady. Alternating current changes direction, so its trace has to cross zero.

optionNotes.option: a wave that stays above the zero line
optionNotes.why: It rises and falls, which looks like a.c., but it never crosses zero, so the current never changes direction.

twin.prompt: A CRO trace crosses the zero line four times across the screen. What does that tell you about the current?
twin.explain: Each crossing of the zero line is a change of direction, so the current changes direction: it is a.c.

optionNotes.why: A one-way current is a flat line that stays on one side of zero; this trace crosses it.
No current is a line along zero. A trace that crosses zero is a current changing direction.

md: A cell's current is steady and flows one way, so its trace is flat and sits on one side of zero. Turn the cell round and the current flows the other way round the circuit: still one way, still steady, but now on the other side of zero.

prompt: A CRO is joined to a battery. What should its trace look like?
options: a flat line above the zero line
a wave that crosses the zero line
a flat line along the zero line
answer: a flat line above the zero line
explain: Step 2 of the See it: a battery's current flows one way and stays steady, so its trace is flat on one side of zero. A wave crossing zero is a.c., and a line along zero means no current. So: a flat line above the zero line.

optionNotes.option: a wave that crosses the zero line
optionNotes.why: That is the mains' a.c. In Summer 2025 many sketched this wave for d.c.; a battery's current never changes direction.

optionNotes.option: a flat line along the zero line
optionNotes.why: Flat is right, but along zero means no current at all. A battery drives a current, so the line sits off zero.

twin.prompt: A CRO is joined to a solar cell in bright light. What should its trace look like?
options: a flat line on one side of the zero line
a wave that crosses the zero line
a flat line along the zero line
twin.answer: a flat line on one side of the zero line
twin.explain: A solar cell gives d.c.: one direction, steady, so a flat line on one side of zero.

optionNotes.option: a wave that crosses the zero line
optionNotes.why: Only a.c. crosses zero; a solar cell's current flows one way.

optionNotes.option: a flat line along the zero line
optionNotes.why: A line along zero means no current; in bright light the solar cell drives one.

prompt: The cell is joined to the CRO the other way round. Which screen, A to D, shows its current now?
explain: Follow steps 1 to 3 of the See it: turning the cell round reverses the current, but it still flows one way and stays steady, so the trace is still flat, now below the zero line: screen A. Screen B is the trace before it was turned round; C crosses zero, so it is a.c.; D is no current.

optionNotes.why: B is the cell before it was turned round. Reversing the current moves the flat line to the other side of zero.
C crosses the zero line, so its current changes direction: a.c. A cell turned round still gives d.c.
D lies on the zero line: no current. The turned cell still drives a current, the other way.

twin.prompt: In the four screens, which one shows a current that keeps changing direction?
twin.explain: A current that changes direction crosses the zero line: screen C. A and B are flat, one way each, and D is no current.

optionNotes.why: A is flat below zero: one direction only, d.c.
B is flat above zero: one direction only, d.c.
D is on the zero line: no current at all.

md: A switch makes or breaks the circuit. It goes in the **live** wire, so that switching off cuts the appliance off from the supply. A switch in the neutral wire stops the current too, but leaves everything inside **still joined to the live wire**, so it could still give a shock.

stem: Two fans are switched off. Fan X has its switch in the live wire; fan Y has its switch in the neutral wire. Which one is safe to open up and touch inside, and why? [2]

steps.working: Fan X: the switch has cut it off from the live supply, so nothing inside is at 230 V.
steps.decision: A switch in the live wire disconnects everything beyond it.

steps.working: Fan Y: no current flows, but the live wire still reaches its motor.
steps.decision: The switch is on the return side, so the live side is untouched.

steps.working: So only fan X is safe to touch inside.
steps.decision: That is why the switch always goes in the live wire.

prompt: A lamp's switch has been fitted in the neutral wire and is turned off. Why is this dangerous?
options: the lamp is still joined to the live wire
the current through the lamp becomes too high
answer: the lamp is still joined to the live wire
explain: Step 2 of the See it: with the switch off in the neutral wire, no current flows, but the live wire still reaches the appliance. The lamp goes dark yet is still joined to the live wire, so touching its insides could give a shock. That is why the switch belongs in the live wire.

optionNotes.why: The lamp does go out: the circuit is broken. The danger is quieter than that: its insides are still joined to the live wire.

optionNotes.option: the current through the lamp becomes too high
optionNotes.why: No current flows once the switch is off. The danger is the live connection left behind, not a big current.

twin.prompt: A heater's switch is fitted in its live wire and is turned off. What is true of the heater's insides?
options: they are cut off from the live supply
they are still joined to the live wire
twin.answer: they are cut off from the live supply
twin.explain: A switch in the live wire disconnects everything beyond it from the supply, so nothing inside is live.

optionNotes.option: they are still joined to the live wire
optionNotes.why: That happens when the switch is in the neutral wire. In the live wire, the switch cuts the live supply off.
With the switch off, no current flows at all.

md:
Each wire in a plug has its own colour, pin and job:
**Live.** Brown, to the bottom right, through the fuse. It brings the supply in.
**Neutral.** Blue, to the bottom left. It completes the circuit.
**Earth.** Green and yellow, to the top pin. A safety wire, joined to a metal case.
The **cable grip** clamps the cable so no wire can be pulled loose.

stem: Wire a plug for a new metal-cased toaster: which wire goes to which terminal? [3]

steps.working: Brown, the live: to the bottom-right terminal, which the fuse sits beside.
steps.decision: The fuse must be on the live side, the wire that brings the supply in.

steps.working: Blue, the neutral: to the bottom-left terminal.
steps.decision: It completes the circuit.

steps.working: Green and yellow, the earth: to the top pin, then the cable grip clamped over the cable.
steps.decision: The toaster's metal case needs its safety route to earth.

prompt: The fuse in a plug has melted. Which wire's path to its pin is now broken?
options: the green and yellow earth wire
explain: Step 1 of the See it: the fuse sits by the bottom-right terminal, and the brown live wire goes there. So a melted fuse breaks the live wire's path, which is the point of it: it cuts off the wire that brings the supply in.

optionNotes.why: The neutral goes to the bottom-left pin, away from the fuse, so a melted fuse leaves its path whole.

optionNotes.option: the green and yellow earth wire
optionNotes.why: The earth goes straight to the top pin. A melted fuse must never break the safety route to earth.

twin.prompt: A plug's fuse has melted. Which pin does the wire it now cuts off lead to?
twin.explain: The fuse sits by the bottom-right terminal, on the brown live wire, so that is the path it breaks.

optionNotes.why: The top pin is the earth's, and the fuse is not on the earth wire.
The bottom-left pin is the neutral's; the fuse is on the live side.

stem: A metal-cased kettle develops a fault: its live wire touches the case. What happens if its earth wire is missing, and what happens when it is connected? [4]

steps.working: No earth wire: the case becomes live, and stays live until someone touches it.
steps.decision: The near-miss: without the earth route nothing makes the fuse melt, so the danger waits for the user.

steps.working: With the earth wire: a very large current flows from the live wire through the case to earth.
steps.decision: The earth wire is an easy route, so the current is far bigger than normal.

steps.working: That large current passes through the fuse and heats its thin wire until it melts.
steps.decision: The fuse is in the live wire, so the fault current goes through it.

steps.working: The circuit is broken and the live supply is cut off, so the case is safe.
steps.decision: What melting achieves: the case is no longer live.

title: GCSE Physics - Fuses & Earthing
why: The fault, the earth wire and the melting fuse, animated. Circuit breakers and residual current devices may appear: they are not on the CCEA specification.

prompt: A lamp has an earthed metal base. A fault joins its live wire to the base. Which way does the large fault current flow?
options: from the live wire, through the base, down the earth wire
from the neutral wire, through the base, down the earth wire
from the earth wire, through the base, into the live wire
answer: from the live wire, through the base, down the earth wire
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, the fault current starts where the supply comes in, the live wire, crosses the metal it touches, and takes the easy route to earth down the earth wire. That large current is what melts the fuse.

optionNotes.option: from the neutral wire, through the base, down the earth wire
optionNotes.why: The neutral is the return path, near 0 V; it pushes nothing. The fault joins the live wire to the base.

optionNotes.option: from the earth wire, through the base, into the live wire
optionNotes.why: It runs the path backwards. The supply's push is in the live wire, so the current flows from live to earth.

twin.prompt: In that fault, where is the fuse that melts?
twin.explain: The fuse sits in the live wire, so the fault current, which starts in the live wire, passes through it and melts it.

optionNotes.why: A fuse in the earth wire would break the safety route itself. The fuse is on the live side.
The fault current never reaches the neutral wire, so a fuse there would not melt.

md: A three-mark question on how a fuse protects is marked as a chain: the **current becomes too high**, the **fuse melts**, and the **circuit is broken**, so the current stops. Melting is the middle link; the first mark needs the cause and the last needs what melting achieves.

title: Where the marks went
md: **Summer 2024:** no question on that paper was answered worse. Most candidates wrote that the fuse melted and stopped there: one mark of three.

stem: Two answers to 'Describe how a fuse protects a hair straightener if a fault develops. [3]' Answer P: 'The fuse melts.' Answer Q: 'The current gets far too big, so the fuse wire melts and leaves a gap, so no current flows.' Mark them.

steps.working: Answer P names only the melting.
steps.decision: The middle link alone: one mark.

steps.working: Answer Q gives the cause first: the current gets far too big.
steps.decision: The first link: a mark.

steps.working: Answer Q then melts the wire and leaves a gap, so no current flows.
steps.decision: The melting and what it achieves: two more marks, three in all.

prompt: A three-mark answer on how a fuse protects an appliance says: 'The current becomes too high and the fuse melts.' Which line would earn the missing mark?
options: The circuit is broken, so the current stops.
The fuse absorbs the extra current.
The fuse is in the live wire.
answer: The circuit is broken, so the current stops.
explain: Answer Q in step 3 of the See it earned its last mark for what melting achieves: a gap, so no current. The answer given has the first two links; the missing one is that the circuit is broken, so the current stops. A fuse absorbs nothing, and where it sits describes nothing it does.

optionNotes.option: The fuse absorbs the extra current.
optionNotes.why: It sounds like protection, but a fuse stores nothing: it melts, and the gap it leaves stops the current.

optionNotes.option: The fuse is in the live wire.
optionNotes.why: True, but it says where the fuse is, not what its melting does. The last mark is for the broken circuit.

twin.prompt: An answer says: 'The fuse melts and the circuit breaks.' Which line would earn the missing mark?
twin.explain: The chain is: current too high, fuse melts, circuit broken. The answer has the last two links; the missing one is the cause, a current that is too high.

optionNotes.why: Getting hot is part of melting, which the answer already has. The missing link is what makes it hot: too high a current.
That repeats the effect in other words. The missing mark is the cause: the current becomes too high.

md: Some appliances, like most hairdryers, have a **plastic** case. Plastic is an insulator, so a loose live wire could never make the outside live. With nothing for an earth wire to protect, the cable has **no earth wire**: only live and neutral. These appliances are **double insulated** and carry the double-square symbol.

stem: A metal-cased iron and a plastic-cased hairdryer each have a loose live wire inside. Which needs an earth wire, and why? [2]

steps.working: The iron: a loose live wire can make its metal case live, so it needs the earth wire.
steps.decision: Metal conducts: the earth route is what protects its user.

steps.working: The hairdryer: its plastic case cannot become live, so it needs no earth; its cable has live and neutral only.
steps.decision: An insulating case is the protection itself.

steps.working: Double insulated does not mean two layers of insulation on the wires.
steps.decision: The near-miss answer: Summer 2024 examiners saw it often.

prompt: A plug is being fitted to a double-insulated drill. Which wire goes to the plug's top pin?
options: the green and yellow earth wire
explain: Step 2 of the See it: an appliance with a plastic case cannot become live, so it has no earth to join. The top pin is the earth's, so for a double-insulated drill nothing goes there: its cable has live and neutral only.

optionNotes.option: the green and yellow earth wire
optionNotes.why: That is where the earth goes in an earthed appliance. A double-insulated drill has no earth wire at all.
The live goes to the bottom-right pin, through the fuse, in every plug.

twin.prompt: How many wires are in the cable of a double-insulated food processor?
options: four: two live and two neutral
twin.explain: With a plastic case there is nothing for an earth wire to protect, so the cable has live and neutral only.

optionNotes.why: Three wires is an earthed, metal-cased appliance. Double insulated means no earth wire.

optionNotes.option: four: two live and two neutral
optionNotes.why: 'Double' is about the insulation, not the number of wires.

title: Why just above the current
md: Below the normal current, a fuse melts in normal use. Far above it, a fuse may not melt in a fault. The smallest fuse above the current does both jobs.

steps.working: $P = I \times V$
steps.decision: The equation first: it earns a mark of its own.
Substitute the power and the mains voltage.
Divide the power by the voltage.

steps.working: 3 A is below 3.5 A, so the fuse is 5 A
steps.decision: The smallest fuse above the normal current.

prompt: A food mixer is rated 368 W and runs on the 230 V mains. What is its normal current, in amps?
explain: As in step 3 of the See it, divide the power by the voltage: I = P ÷ V = 368 ÷ 230 = 1.6 A. Its fuse would then be 3 A, the smallest above 1.6 A.

steps.working: $P = I \times V$
steps.decision: The equation first.
Kilowatts to watts: multiply by 1000.
Divide the power in watts by the voltage.

steps.working: 11 A is above 5 A, so the fuse is 13 A
steps.decision: The smallest fuse above the current.

prompt: A heater is rated 1.38 kW and runs on the 230 V mains. What is its normal current, in amps?
explain: Convert first, as in step 2 of the See it: 1.38 kW = 1380 W. Then I = 1380 ÷ 230 = 6 A. Left in kilowatts, 1.38 ÷ 230 gives a current 1000 times too small. Its fuse would be 13 A.

steps.decision: Cross out any fuse smaller than the normal current first.

steps.working: Above 1.4 A: 2 A and 5 A. The smallest of those: 2 A.
steps.decision: The same rule on any list: the smallest fuse above the current.

prompt: A question offers 1 A, 3 A and 5 A fuses for an appliance whose normal current is 2.2 A. Which fuse should be chosen?

steps.decision: Divide both sides by V.

steps.decision: The Vs on the right cancel, leaving I.

prompt: Rearrange P = I × V to give the voltage V.
explain: Do what steps 2 and 3 of the See it did, dividing by the other letter: divide both sides of P = I × V by I, the Is cancel, and V = P ÷ I. Check the units: watts ÷ amperes = volts.

optionNotes.why: It divides the right letters the wrong way up: the slip that makes a bigger power give a smaller voltage.
Multiplying undoes nothing: to get V alone you divide both sides by I.

twin.prompt: An appliance takes a current I from the mains at voltage V. Which expression gives its power P?
twin.explain: Power is current times voltage: P = I × V. The other two are divisions, which belong to rearranging it.

optionNotes.why: Power is the product of current and voltage, not a quotient.
V ÷ I is the resistance, not the power.
